strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: reusing vision token hidden states via logit-lens projection as internal reference signals for decoding is a novel twist within the intra-alignment family, and the observation that vocabulary constraining is needed to make vision-token projections informative (Figure 2, Section 2.3) is an interesting empirical finding in itself.

Strong efficiency story: the method is training-free, requires no extra forward passes, and achieves only 2.3-3.5% latency overhead versus roughly 2x for VCD/M3ID/SID, validated with per-token latency measurements (Table 7, Figure 3). This directly supports the paper's central claim.

Broad and mostly careful evaluation: CHAIR, POPE (all 18 settings reported in full), and AMBER across LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, plus a MoE model (DeepSeek-VL2), demonstrating architectural generality. ReVisiT beats greedy across all 18 POPE settings, which is a nontrivial consistency result given baselines sometimes underperform greedy.

Good transparency and reproducibility support: full pseudo-code (Algorithm 1), fixed seeds, detailed benchmark setups in the appendix, an ablation over vocabulary constraint / layer selection / alpha, detailed case-study tables with exact logits (Tables 8-10), and honest failure-case examples (Appendix C.2).
The paper is honest about limitations (overfitting to visually salient cues, no external knowledge) and situates the work well relative to pre-/intra-/post-alignment methods.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter selection protocol is a soundness concern: the layer-selection strategy is fixed per model ('last' vs. 'all even-numbered layers') and the APC threshold alpha is 'set for each task', spanning 1e-1 to 1e-6. There is no described validation set or held-out selection procedure, so per-task tuning appears to be done on the evaluation benchmarks themselves. This weakens the claim of consistent superiority, especially given some margins are small (e.g., POPE accuracy 84.77 vs. 84.49 greedy on Qwen2.5-VL; several POPE cells are within noise of SID).

Gains on the stronger model (Qwen2.5-VL) are modest and mixed outside CHAIR: e.g., Hal on AMBER worsens relative to greedy on LLaVA-1.5 side metrics, and several baselines' behavior on Qwen suggests the method's benefit may be concentrated on models with weaker grounding. No significance testing or confidence intervals accompany the benchmark tables.

The efficiency claim hinges on caching lvision of size |J| x |v| x |V|. For high-resolution models (Qwen2.5-VL with many vision tokens) and multiple layers over a ~150k vocabulary, this cache can be very large; the paper reports latency but does not report or discuss GPU memory overhead, which is the natural cost of the precomputation trick.

Theoretical justification is thin: selecting the vision token that minimizes JSD to the current output distribution, then multiplying distributions, is an effective heuristic, but the paper offers limited principled reasoning for why minimum-divergence selection (rather than, e.g., maximum divergence or attention-based selection) is the right criterion, and no analysis of when it fails.

The degenerate behavior in the w/o-subset ablation ( Recall 0.83, severe repetition) shows the method is unstable without a tightly tuned constraint, which slightly undercuts the 'simple, robust free lunch' framing; the sensitivity to alpha is acknowledged but not fully characterized across models/tasks.

Writing has recurring grammatical issues ('this constraint reduce', 'we refer logit-lens as'), and the Figure 2 motivation relies on a manually defined vocabulary subset, which is illustrative but anecdotal; a quantitative version of that motivation (e.g., how often constrained vision-token projections rank ground-truth objects higher) would strengthen Section 2.3.
No mention of releasing code, which limits reproducibility of a method whose performance depends on nontrivial implementation choices (slicing/masking of cached projections, layer pooling).

strengths: The proposed method is genuinely training-free and model-agnostic, requiring no additional forward passes; the precomputed vision-token projection cache is a clean and sensible engineering design that supports the central efficiency claim.

Evaluation coverage is broad: three hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, AMBER) across three LVLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, DeepSeekVL2-MoE), with the MoE experiment adding evidence of architectural generality.

The efficiency analysis is a real differentiator: ReVisiT adds only ~2-3.5% latency versus greedy decoding, while all compared intra-alignment baselines roughly double computation, and the paper honestly reports DoLa's overhead.

Reproducibility support is above average: seeds are specified, prompts are stated, hyperparameters and layer-selection strategies are documented, a full algorithmic specification is given (Algorithm 1), and detailed token-level numerical case studies (Tables 8-10) let readers verify the mechanism end-to-end.

The motivation section is thoughtful: the taxonomy of pre/intra/post-alignment is clear, and the observation that hallucinations often have grounded alternatives in the top-K candidates is a reasonable and interesting starting point.
weaknesses: The 'free lunch' framing is overstated. The APC threshold α is set per task, and the layer-selection strategy differs per model ('last' for LLaVA-1.5 vs. 'all even layers' for Qwen2.5-VL). Tuning on the evaluated benchmarks undermines the claim of a hyperparameter-light, plug-and-play method; sensitivity to these choices is shown in the ablation but not characterized on held-out settings.

Gains over the strongest baseline (SID) are modest and sometimes within noise: on CHAIRs for LLaVA-1.5 the result ties (50.6), on POPE F1 for Qwen2.5-VL SID is higher (83.30 vs. 83.18), and no statistical significance testing is reported for any comparison.

The mechanism selection (minimizing JSD between the output distribution and each vision-token projection) is motivated only qualitatively. There is no quantitative evidence that the JSD criterion reliably identifies visually relevant tokens rather than merely low-information ones, and no analysis of how often the selected token actually corrects versus perturbs the prediction.

The core technique is an incremental combination of known ideas: logit-lens projection, DoLa-style internal reference logits, adaptive vocabulary constriction from contrastive decoding, and probability-product fusion. The novelty lies in applying these to vision tokens, which is reasonable but not a substantial conceptual advance.

There is an explicit coverage-hallucination trade-off that is downplayed: Recall drops on Qwen2.5-VL CHAIR (71.79 to 70.83) and DeepSeekVL2 (59.51 to 57.49), suggesting the method partly suppresses mentions rather than improving grounding per se.

The vocabulary-constraint ablation result (CHAIRs = 0.2 with Recall = 0.83 without the subset) reveals the method can catastrophically collapse generation; while the failure cases are helpfully shown, the paper does not provide any safeguard or analysis of when such degeneration occurs.

Evaluation is confined to object-level hallucination metrics; the method's effect on general caption quality, fluency, or non-object hallucination types (attribute/relation in AMBER's discriminative setting) is not measured, so the scope of the claimed 'enhanced visual grounding' is narrower than the framing suggests.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the taxonomy of pre-/intra-/post-alignment is useful, and the insight of repurposing vision token hidden states (via logit-lens style projection) as internal reference signals for visual grounding is intuitive and well supported by the motivating analysis in Section 2.3 and Figure 2.

The method is genuinely lightweight: no training, no extra forward passes, no external models; projections are precomputed once and per-step cost is only JSD computation and masking over the constrained vocabulary, supported by careful latency measurements (Table 7: ~2-3% overhead vs. ~2x for baselines).

Broad and reasonably rigorous empirical validation: three hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, AMBER) plus qualitative LLaVA-Bench examples, three models spanning dense (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL) and sparse MoE (DeepSeek-VL2) architectures, and consistent improvements over greedy decoding across nearly all 18 POPE settings.

Ablations isolate each design choice (vocabulary constraint, layer pool, threshold alpha), and the degenerate w/o-subset case is honestly reported and analyzed rather than hidden, with failure cases shown in Appendix C.2.
Good reproducibility support: full pseudocode (Algorithm 1), hyperparameter ranges, seeds, prompt templates, dataset construction details, and per-figure numerical breakdowns in the appendix.
Writing is clear and the paper is well organized; limitations and broader impacts are thoughtfully discussed.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter tuning transparency is a concern: the APC threshold alpha is 'set for each task' and the layer pool differs per model, with limited discussion of how these were chosen (risk of test-set tuning). Given that alpha strongly affects results in Table 4, this weakens the claim of a 'free lunch'.

Margins over the strongest baseline (SID) are often small and reported without statistical significance tests or variance across seeds (e.g., POPE on Qwen2.5-VL differs by ~0.01-0.3 points; CHAIR_S ties SID on LLaVA-1.5). Single-run results make some claims hard to distinguish from noise.

Baseline coverage is somewhat narrow: HALC, OPERA, DAMRO, and other recent intra-alignment methods cited in Section 5.3 are not empirically compared, so 'state-of-the-art' claims rest on four baselines (VCD, M3ID, SID, DoLa).

The contribution is largely an assembly of existing components (logit-lens projection, adaptive plausible-context vocabulary from [38], JSD-based selection as in DoLa, multiplicative logit fusion); the element-wise multiplication refinement is heuristic and lacks theoretical or analytical justification for why this fusion form is preferred over interpolation or contrastive subtraction.

The 'up to 2x computational cost reduction' framing compares against the cost of slower baselines rather than demonstrating an absolute efficiency gain over greedy decoding; the headline could be read as slightly overstated.

Some generative outputs (e.g., Figure 4, ReVisiT row) show residual artifacts and abrupt references, suggesting the quality gain in open-ended generation is not uniformly clean; open-ended quality is only qualitatively assessed.
No explicit statement of code release, which limits practical reproducibility despite the detailed setups.

strengths: The motivation section provides genuinely informative empirical analyses: (i) GT objects remain among top-k candidates at hallucinated steps (95.8% recall@500 with Wilson CIs), and (ii) vision-token projections over semantically coherent vocabulary subsets reveal object-level semantics (40.44% top-1 recall vs 2.03% on full vocabulary). These analyses are supported by statistical rigor (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Holm-adjusted p-values, Wilson intervals) that exceeds the norm for this paper type.

ReVisiT is a simple, training-free, model-agnostic decoding method with essentially zero overhead (+1.9%/+0.6% vs greedy), a genuine practical advantage over contrastive-decoding baselines (VCD, M3ID, CODE, SID) that cost ~2x or more; the efficiency comparison is well-designed (300 samples, warmups, std. deviations).

Broad and mostly convincing empirical validation: five benchmarks spanning hallucination (CHAIR, POPE, HallusionBench) and general VQA (VQAv2, MMMU), six/seven model sizes across three architectures, six competitive baselines, and thorough ablations (selection criterion, vocabulary constraint, layer scope, threshold α).

Reproducibility is well supported: fixed seeds, official evaluation scripts, explicit metrics/formulas (including a per-sample F1 definition), full pseudo-code (Algorithm 1), hyperparameter ranges, and detailed case-study numerical values in the appendix.

Clear writing and a coherent narrative connecting analysis findings (constrained projection reveals latent visual semantics) to the method design (adaptive vocabulary constraint + min-JSD token selection + multiplicative logit refinement); ablations directly validate each design choice (e.g., full-vocab min-JSD collapses to F1=1.52).
weaknesses: Hyperparameter tuning practice raises fairness and generalization concerns: α is 'set for each task,' and layer scope differs per model, while baselines use default settings; there is no description of tuning on held-out data, so test-set tuning cannot be ruled out and the modest robustness claims (sensitivity within ~1.5 F1) rest on a single benchmark (CHAIR/Qwen).

Results are not uniformly consistent with the 'consistently improves' claim: on LLaVA-1.5-13B, CHAIR_S degrades substantially (48.0 → 52.6), and gains on Qwen2.5-VL-32B are marginal; on POPE, SID beats ReVisiT on several individual setups (e.g., MS-COCO Random/Popular on Qwen), and several Table 4 improvements are within noise with no significance testing reported for the main benchmark tables.

The headline 'reducing computational cost by up to 2×' is somewhat overstated — the method simply matches greedy decoding cost while baselines are slower; it does not reduce cost relative to any baseline.

The core motivation analyses are conducted on a single model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and a small step-level sample (n=190 hallucinated steps from 500 COCO images), leaving the generality of the analysis findings under-supported; the conceptual vocabulary subsets (e.g., V_env) are manually defined, which weakens the interpretability claims' objectivity.

Methodological justification is thin in places: min-JSD selects the vision token whose distribution is closest to the output distribution, which is only heuristically argued to be the 'most relevant'; no comparison with alternative relevance criteria beyond max-JSD/random, and no theoretical or attention-based grounding for why the closest projection is the best reference. The coarse-then-fine dynamic selection mentioned in the abstract is not clearly reflected in the method description.

Minor presentation issues reduce polish: typos ('Referecing', 'he best results', 'validiate', 'its constrained projection'), inconsistent claims between abstract and Table 9, and some figure/axis descriptions (Figure 1 y-axis truncation) that could mislead.

strengths: The motivating analyses are quantitative and reasonably careful: at-least-one recall@k with Wilson confidence intervals, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction for the w/image vs. w/o-image comparison, and clear metric definitions (Appendix A.1). This is above-average statistical rigor for decoding-method papers.

Breadth of empirical evaluation is substantial: five benchmarks (HallusionBench, CHAIR, POPE, MMMU, VQAv2), seven models across three architectures, six decoding baselines, latency measurements, and ablations over four design factors.
The method is training-free, model-agnostic, and essentially overhead-free (+1.9%/+0.6% latency), which is a practical advantage over multi-pass baselines like VCD/M3ID/CODE.

Implementation details, hyperparameters, evaluation protocols (fixed seeds, official benchmark code), and per-case numerical breakdowns (Tables 13-15) are documented in enough detail to support reproducibility, and ablations honestly show the method fails under full-vocabulary projection or max-JSD selection.
weaknesses: Hyperparameters appear to be tuned on the test benchmarks. The layer scope differs per model ('mostly' the last layer for LLaVA, 'all even-numbered layers' for Qwen) and alpha is 'set for each task' across all five benchmarks, apparently selected on the evaluation sets themselves. This severely weakens the claims of a simple, hyperparameter-light, model-agnostic method, and makes cross-method comparisons favor the proposed method.

The second motivating analysis (Sec. 2.2, Fig. 4) is partially circular: the 'semantically coherent' constrained subset is exactly the CHAIR-derived object vocabulary (the 176 synonyms covering the 62 GT categories), and recall is then measured against GT synonyms within those categories. Restricting the candidate set to (nearly) the label set naturally inflates recall; the comparison is made fairer by restricting GT targets to the same 62 categories, but the headline '20x improvement' framing overstates what is a largely mechanical effect of shrinking the candidate space.

The claims of 'consistent improvements' (Fig. 1) are not fully supported by the paper's own results: Table 9 shows CHAIR_S degrading on LLaVA-1.5-13B (48.0 to 52.6), negligible change on Qwen2.5-VL-32B, and SID beating ReVisiT on several POPE settings (e.g., MS-COCO Random/Popular accuracy on Qwen). The narrative oversells uniformity.

The abstract's claim of 'reducing computational cost by up to 2x' is misleading: ReVisiT does not reduce cost relative to greedy decoding (it adds ~1-2%); the 2x figure refers to other baselines being slower. This is an important presentation issue for a headline claim.

Main benchmark results are single-run point estimates with no variance or significance testing, while the motivating analyses do get CIs; the large qAcc jump on HallusionBench (11.55 to 20.22) is on a small benchmark and deserves uncertainty quantification.

The vision-token reference distributions are cached from the initial forward pass and never updated during generation, so 'context-aware' applies only to subset construction and selection; the method's interaction with long generations (e.g., 512-token captions) is not analyzed.

The core mechanism (element-wise multiplication with a logit-lens-style projection of one selected vision token) is simple and somewhat ad hoc; effectiveness depends heavily on the APC constraint (full-vocab variant collapses to F1=1.52), suggesting fragility rather than a robust grounding mechanism, and the contribution relative to logit-lens analysis (nostalgebraist, Chuang et al.) and existing intra-alignment decoding is incremental.

Numerous writing and consistency issues: 'he best results' typo, 'presentation of image', inconsistent notation between probability and log-probability columns in Table 13, and grammar errors throughout, indicating the manuscript was not carefully polished.

strengths: The motivation section provides unusually careful empirical analysis for a decoding paper: at-least-one recall@k with Wilson confidence intervals, a w/o-image ablation isolating the contribution of vision tokens, and appropriate nonparametric statistics (Wilcoxon signed-rank with Holm correction) to support the claim that vision tokens carry grounding signal.

The proposed method (ReVisiT) is simple, training-free, model-agnostic, and clearly specified: adaptive vocabulary constraining, JSD-based vision-token selection, and probability-product refinement are each explicitly formulated, with full pseudo-code (Algorithm 1) and precomputed-projection implementation details that support reproducibility.

Evaluation breadth is a decisive strength: five benchmarks spanning generative and discriminative settings, six-to-seven model sizes across three architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL), and six strong intra-alignment decoding baselines (DoLa, VCD, M3ID, CODE, SID).
The efficiency analysis is compelling and well-executed: near-greedy latency (+0.6% to +1.9%) versus roughly 2x overhead for competing decoding methods, with latency tables and hardware specified.

The ablation study directly validates each design choice (min-JSD vs. random/max selection, subset vs. full vocabulary, layer scope, threshold alpha), and failure cases without the vocabulary constraint are shown qualitatively.

Reproducibility provisions are good: fixed sampling seed, official benchmark implementations and protocols, metric definitions in the appendix, hyperparameter ranges documented, and per-model layer/threshold settings stated.
weaknesses: Potential test-set hyperparameter tuning: the APC threshold alpha is 'set for each task' while baselines use their default hyperparameters, and the layer-scope setting is chosen per model ('mostly' last layer vs. even layers). This asymmetry weakens the fairness of the head-to-head comparisons and the main-conference-level claims; results with a single fixed default alpha across all tasks should be reported.

The headline motivating result (Sec 2.2, Fig 4) is partly by construction: comparing recall@k of a 176-token constrained subset against the full 151k vocabulary inflates the constrained numbers largely through base rates. The more informative baseline (recall relative to random chance within the subset) is not reported, so the '20x' framing overstates what the analysis establishes about latent semantics.

Gains are modest and inconsistent on several settings: CHAIR_S worsens for LLaVA-1.5-13B (48.0 -> 52.6), POPE accuracy on Qwen2.5-VL trails SID, and some model sizes show near-zero improvements, which sits in some tension with the 'consistent improvements' framing; no significance testing or variance reporting accompanies the main benchmark tables (HallusionBench's large qAcc jump over all baselines is unexplained).

The 'up to 2x' computational cost reduction claim is relative to other hallucination-mitigation decoding methods, not to standard greedy decoding; the framing could mislead readers about the method's absolute cost.

There is an internal inconsistency between the main text (Eq. 6: element-wise multiplication of probabilities) and Appendix C.1 ('log-probability fusion'); multiplying probabilities and adding log-probabilities produce materially different refined distributions, and the paper should clarify which is actually used.

The memory footprint of caching the |J| x |v| x |V| projection matrix (e.g., for 26-32B models with ~150k vocabularies and many vision tokens) is never discussed and could be substantial; the practicality claim at larger scales is under-supported.

Novelty is moderate: adaptive plausibility constraints are taken from prior contrastive-decoding work (Li et al., 2023a), the projection analysis is a logit-lens analogue, and the refinement is a multiplicative logit adjustment; the genuinely new component is the context-aware JSD-based vision-token selection, and the paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of the delta over SID/M3ID-style vision-referencing decoders.

The CHAIR F1 analysis shows method-dependent trade-offs (e.g., CODE achieves far lower CHAIR_S with collapsed F1) that are not deeply analyzed; a discussion of why ReVisiT lands where it does on the precision-recall frontier is missing.
